title: Atrial fibrillation: rapid ventricular rate, rhythm control and anticoagulation
subject: cardiology
summary: Cardiovert immediately if unstable; otherwise control rate (initial target below 110/min) with a beta-blocker, diltiazem or verapamil (LVEF above 40%) or digoxin, delay cardioversion beyond 24 hours unless anticoagulated for 3 weeks or TOE-cleared, and anticoagulate with a DOAC when CHA2DS2-VA is 2 or more.

sections.title: Recognise and classify
items: Irregularly irregular narrow-complex rhythm without distinct P waves on a 12-lead ECG (or a 30-second single-lead strip). Irregular broad-complex tachycardia at very fast rates suggests pre-excited AF (WPW).
Classify: first diagnosed, paroxysmal (ends within 7 days), persistent (over 7 days), permanent (rhythm control no longer pursued).
Unstable features needing immediate cardioversion: hypotension or shock, acute pulmonary oedema, ongoing ischaemia, syncope.
Look for triggers: sepsis, thyrotoxicosis, alcohol, hypokalaemia or hypomagnesaemia, pulmonary embolism, acute MI, post-operative state, and in India rheumatic mitral valve disease.

sections.title: Acute management
items: Haemodynamically unstable: urgent synchronised DC cardioversion under sedation; start heparin without delaying the shock. If cardioversion fails or AF recurs, IV amiodarone for rate control.
Stable with rapid rate: treat the trigger, then rate control. Initial target resting heart rate below 110/min (lenient), tighter if symptoms persist.
LVEF above 40%: beta-blocker, diltiazem or verapamil, or digoxin. LVEF 40% or less or decompensated HF: beta-blocker and/or digoxin; avoid diltiazem and verapamil.
Pre-excited AF (WPW): do not give AV nodal blockers (adenosine, beta-blockers, diltiazem, verapamil, digoxin) or IV amiodarone; DC cardioversion if unstable, otherwise specialist advice.
Start anticoagulation early (LMWH or DOAC) in patients being considered for cardioversion or with CHA2DS2-VA of 2 or more, unless contraindicated.

sections.title: Investigations
items: 12-lead ECG, CBC, creatinine and creatinine clearance (Cockcroft-Gault for DOAC dosing), electrolytes including magnesium, liver function, TSH, glucose.
Echocardiography: LVEF (guides drug choice), valve disease (mitral stenosis, prosthetic valves), left atrial size.
Troponin only if acute coronary syndrome is suspected (modest rises are common with fast rates). Chest X-ray or other tests for the trigger as indicated.

sections.title: Rhythm control and cardioversion
items: Safety first: if AF has lasted over 24 hours (or duration is unknown), do not cardiovert without at least 3 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation or a TOE that excludes left atrial thrombus.
Recent-onset stable AF: a wait-and-see approach with rate control is reasonable, as many episodes end spontaneously within 48 hours; cardiovert if AF persists and the patient is symptomatic.

Pharmacological cardioversion: flecainide or propafenone only if there is no significant structural or ischaemic heart disease, LVH or reduced LVEF; amiodarone if structural heart disease or heart failure.
Continue anticoagulation for at least 4 weeks after cardioversion, and long term according to CHA2DS2-VA, whatever the rhythm outcome.
Consider early rhythm control (antiarrhythmic drugs or catheter ablation) within 12 months of diagnosis in selected patients; catheter ablation is an option first-line for symptomatic paroxysmal AF.

sections.title: Stroke prevention: anticoagulation
items: CHA2DS2-VA (ESC 2024, sex removed): congestive heart failure 1, hypertension 1, age 75 or older 2, diabetes 1, prior stroke, TIA or thromboembolism 2, vascular disease 1, age 65 to 74 1.

Score 2 or more: oral anticoagulation recommended. Score 1: anticoagulation should be considered. Score 0: no anticoagulation. ACC/AHA 2023 uses CHA2DS2-VASc (anticoagulate at 2 or more in men and 3 or more in women).
Prefer a DOAC over a VKA, at full dose unless the drug-specific dose-reduction criteria are met. Do not under-dose.

Use a VKA (warfarin or acenocoumarol, INR 2.0 to 3.0) for mechanical heart valves and moderate to severe mitral stenosis (common rheumatic cause in India); DOACs are contraindicated in these patients.

Do not use aspirin or other antiplatelets as a substitute for anticoagulation. Do not withhold anticoagulation because of a bleeding score; instead correct modifiable bleeding risks (BP, alcohol, NSAIDs, antiplatelets, labile INR).

sections.title: Special situations
items: CKD: dabigatran is contraindicated if CrCl is below 30 mL/min; avoid DOACs below 15 mL/min or on dialysis except under specialist advice.
Pregnancy: rate control with beta-1 selective beta-blocker or digoxin; LMWH for anticoagulation; electrical cardioversion is safe if unstable.
Thyrotoxicosis: beta-blocker plus antithyroid treatment; anticoagulate by stroke risk.
AF with ACS or PCI: triple therapy (OAC, aspirin, clopidogrel) for up to 1 week, then OAC plus clopidogrel up to 12 months, then OAC alone.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Cardioverting AF of more than 24 hours or unknown duration without anticoagulation or TOE.
Diltiazem or verapamil in reduced LVEF; AV nodal blockers in pre-excited AF.
Reduced-dose DOAC without meeting criteria (under-dosing increases stroke risk).
Giving a DOAC to a patient with rheumatic mitral stenosis or a mechanical valve.

drugs.name: Metoprolol
drugs.dose: 2.5 to 5 mg IV bolus over 2 minutes, repeat up to 4 doses; oral metoprolol tartrate 25 to 100 mg twice daily
drugs.notes: Avoid in decompensated HF, severe asthma, hypotension.

drugs.name: Esmolol
drugs.dose: 500 mcg/kg IV over 1 minute, then 50 to 300 mcg/kg/min infusion
drugs.notes: Short-acting; useful in critically ill or peri-operative patients.

drugs.name: Diltiazem
drugs.dose: 0.25 mg/kg IV over 5 minutes, then 5 to 15 mg/h infusion; oral 60 mg three times daily up to 360 mg/day (modified release once daily)

drugs.name: Verapamil
drugs.dose: 2.5 to 10 mg IV over 5 minutes; oral 40 mg twice daily up to 480 mg/day
drugs.notes: Only if LVEF above 40%. Interacts with dabigatran and digoxin.

drugs.name: Digoxin
drugs.dose: 0.5 mg IV bolus, total 0.75 to 1.5 mg over 24 hours in divided doses; oral maintenance 62.5 to 250 mcg once daily
drugs.notes: Reduce in CKD and elderly. Slow onset; useful in HF and low BP.

drugs.name: Amiodarone
drugs.dose: 300 mg IV in 250 mL 5% glucose over 30 to 60 minutes, then 900 to 1200 mg IV over 24 hours (central line preferred); oral 200 mg three times daily for about 4 weeks then 200 mg daily
drugs.notes: Rate or rhythm control in HF or haemodynamic instability. Can cardiovert, so consider stroke risk. Thyroid, liver, lung toxicity long term.

drugs.name: Apixaban
drugs.dose: 5 mg orally twice daily; 2.5 mg twice daily if 2 of: age 80 or older, weight 60 kg or less, serum creatinine 1.5 mg/dL (133 micromol/L) or more

drugs.name: Rivaroxaban
drugs.dose: 20 mg orally once daily with the evening meal; 15 mg once daily if CrCl 15 to 49 mL/min

drugs.name: Dabigatran
drugs.dose: 150 mg orally twice daily; 110 mg twice daily if age 80 or older or taking verapamil (consider if 75 to 80, CrCl 30 to 50, gastritis or high bleeding risk)

drugs.name: Edoxaban
drugs.dose: 60 mg orally once daily; 30 mg once daily if CrCl 15 to 50 mL/min, weight 60 kg or less, or strong P-gp inhibitor (ciclosporin, dronedarone, erythromycin, ketoconazole)
